title: Doubly linked rings
summary: Circular doubly linked lists with a sentinel, built from `Pref` cells: insertion, removal and reversal in a ring of any length, and moving a range of nodes between two rings. Each operation's contract gives the new model and the exact heap after the call as a few writes to the old one, which also says that every other cell is unchanged. The tour reads the ring predicate, the contracts, a client and a rejected program, then the abstract `Owned` interface, the proofs of insertion, reversal and the range move, the two heap laws the proofs call, and the emitted-code check.
The [catalogue page](demo:rings) states the claim, the trusted base and the scope.

stops.title: A ring is a predicate on a heap
stops.text: A ring node is an immutable record of an `int`, a sentinel flag and two cells, `prev` and `next`, of type `node option Pref.t`. A ring's erased model is its sentinel and the list of its other nodes in forward order: `ring h s ns` says that in heap `h` the sentinel's `next` cell holds the first node, and `linked` checks each node's `prev` and `next` contents along `ns` and finally the sentinel's `prev`. `separated` says that the nodes are distinct, share no cell, and that no node's `prev` and `next` are one cell. Nodes are compared as values, so two node records are equal when they have the same value, flag and cells.

stops.title: Insert, remove, reverse: the exact heap afterwards
stops.text: The caller names a position by splitting the model: `insert` links a new node after `left`, where the model is `append prefix suffix` and `left` is `last sentinel prefix`, and `remove` takes the model `append prefix (n :: suffix)`. Each postcondition gives the new model and the new heap: the old heap after the four link writes of `inserted` or `removed`, or for `reverse` the old heap with every node's `prev` and `next` contents exchanged (`flipped_all`). These are equations on the whole owned heap, so they also say that every other cell keeps its contents. `insert` also promises that the new node's cells were not in the old heap, and `remove` leaves `n` linked to itself, its cells still owned by the token.

stops.title: A client builds and edits a ring
stops.text: The client uses the one-ring `Owned` interface, which hides the ring invariant. `push_front` asks for the sentinel with `sentinel_node` and inserts after it with an empty `prefix`; `pop_front` observes the nodes and removes the first. Each states its result's model, proved from the `Owned` contracts and the `append_def` and `last_def` equations. The main program builds the ring 1, 2, 3, removes the middle node, inserts 4 after the last, reverses the ring and empties it, proving the observed node list after each step and checking the values with `assert` in bytecode and native code.

stops.title: A rejected client: reversal without separation
stops.text: `reverse` requires `separated (sentinel :: ns)`. A caller that knows only `ring (Pref.own t) sentinel ns` is rejected, and the error points at that precondition in `pref_ring_general.mli`. Separation is what lets `reverse_nodes` exchange each node's links independently: if two nodes shared a cell, or a node's `prev` and `next` were one cell, a later write would undo an earlier one. The same test rejects a range move whose `final` is not the last node of the range or whose `destination_left` is misplaced, an insertion at the wrong position, removal of a node outside the model, false claims about the resulting models, reuse of a consumed `Owned.t` or released record, and uses of private proofs.

stops.title: Owned: the ring invariant behind an abstract type
stops.text: `Owned.t` is an unboxed record whose one field refines `payload` by `ring` and `separated`; its layout is `value & void & void`, so at run time it is the sentinel alone. `adopt` proves the invariant once, and each operation of `Owned` assumes it on entry and proves it again for the value it builds. `empty` makes a sentinel whose two cells point at itself and proves it a ring with no other nodes. Clients see `model`, `sentinel` and `heap` without their definitions: they can state the exact heap after an operation but cannot reach the representation.

stops.title: Insertion: allocate, read one link, write four
stops.text: `insert` reads the node after `left` with `read_node`, whose `None` branch ends in `unreachable_ ()`, a branch the checker proves dead from the precondition. `make_node` allocates the new node's two cells and points both at the node, and `insert_between` performs the four link writes. The resulting heap is the old one with eight `put`s, where the contract promises `inserted`, which has four: `allocation_inserted` proves the two equal, since the insertion overwrites both of the new node's cells, and `insert_law` proves the result a separated ring whose model is `append prefix (n :: suffix)`. `Pref_ring_proofs.allocation_frame` records that the allocation leaves the neighbors' cells unchanged.

stops.title: Reversal: exchange every node's links
stops.text: `reverse` borrows the token to `traverse` the ring forward, which returns the node list the model predicts, and passes `sentinel :: nodes` to `Pref_ring.reverse_nodes`, which exchanges each node's `prev` and `next` contents and whose contract is exactly `flipped_all` of the old heap. `reverse_law` proves the ring part: in `flipped_all h (sentinel :: ns)` the same nodes form a separated ring whose model is `reversed ns`. The traversal builds its list with a recursion that is not tail-recursive, so reversal uses stack and space linear in the ring's length.

stops.title: Moving a range between two rings
stops.from: val splice : (s : node) @ immutable ghost -> (t : node) @ immutable ghost ->
stops.text: `splice` takes one token that owns two rings, with sentinels `s` and `t`, and requires the concatenation of their node lists to be `separated`. It removes the nonempty range `first :: rest`, whose last node the caller passes as `final`, from the first ring and inserts it after `destination_left` in the second. The postcondition gives both new models, proves both are rings and still separated together, and states the heap as the old one after six link writes (`spliced`, three applications of `connected`). The implementation reads three links and calls `Pref_ring.splice_range`, with `splice_law` carrying the proof; `Owned.splice` and `Owned.swap` wrap it for a pair of rings, and a move within one ring is outside the scope.

stops.title: The trusted base, and two heap laws
stops.text: Beyond the shared `Pref` base, the C primitives behind `alloc`, `read` and `write` and the checker's encoding of heap terms, the ring proofs call two heap laws, in this lemma only. `commute_law` reorders writes to distinct cells and `put_law` drops a write that a later write to the same cell overrides; `insert` needs them, through `allocation_inserted`, to show that the allocation's writes disappear under the insertion's. `put_law` is an `external`, so each call adds an assumed instance; `commute_law` is proved in `pref.ml`. The other ring proofs rely only on the encoding of `put`, `at` and `mem` and on the contracts of the `Pref` operations.

stops.title: Emitted code: the audited ring functions
stops.text: The check described in the [lists and trees tour](tour:lists-trees/10) covers the ring modules too: [`structures_erasure.ml`](src:testsuite/tests/vox/structures_erasure.ml) compiles them natively with `-dlambda`, and each function named here, with every function of its module that it reaches by name, may call only the runtime functions on a fixed list and no model function, lemma, `_def` equation, `Proofs` member or heap law. The list covers the raw operations of `Pref_ring`, the general `insert`, `remove`, `reverse`, `splice` and `swap`, the `Owned` observers, and the entry points of the older fixed-size demos. Calls into other modules are not followed.
